newsitem.title: CHINA: Law on elderly lends a hand to greying China.
newsitem.headline: Law on elderly lends a hand to greying China.

text.p: China's rapidly growing army of elderly is throwing a heavy burden on society, but Beijing has taken a vital step toward shouldering the weight with a new law banning neglect of the old, officials said on Thursday.

New legal protection of the rights of 120 million Chinese senior citizens showed Beijing was meeting the challenge of a greying population, said Professor Zhang Wenfan, president of the China National Committe on Ageing.
"The ageing population trend that China faces is extremely grim," Zhang said in an interview. "Passing this law signals that China has entered a new stage in its work on ageing."
China's National People's Congress, or parliament, passed the law banning neglect, slander or abuse of senior citizens in a unanimous vote late last month.
The law seeks to bolster China's ancient Confucian tradition of respect for the elderly by ordering families to take responsibility for their oldest members.
China's shifting demography was the result of the success of its family planning policy in cutting population growth coupled with a falling death rate, said Zhang, who is 55.
Almost 120 million Chinese were senior citizens, accounting for 9.6 percent of the population, and their ranks were swelling by around three percent a year, he said.

The number of elderly is expected to rise as high as 410 million during the 21st century, accounting for 27 percent of the population, official statistics show. China considers men over 60 and women over 55 to be senior citizens.

While the majority of China's elderly live in villages and rely mainly on their families, retired urban workers are supported by their former employers -- a heavy burden on state-owned firms struggling to survive in the new sink-or-swim market economy.
"The traditional planned economy system and its social structures, including ... social guarantees for old people, will be pounded and destroyed by the market economy," Zhang said.

Beijing was moving to boost spending on social provisions for old people and was promoting invested pensions and insurance, but families would have to continue to be responsible for much of the financial burden, he added.

Traditional Confucian values demand deep filial piety, but many Chinese say respect for the elderly has declined during four decades of communist rule, which has often prized political correctness more highly than family ties.

Zhang said economic dependency, the shrinking of extended families and the strains of modern life in new apartment blocks which have replaced many small compound-style homes and communities had all helped to diminish the status of senior citizens.
While developed nations were also having to face up to the economic realities of their ageing populations, they had had far more time to prepare than China, he said.
"To put it simply, they were first rich, then old," Zhang said. "But China is still a developing country, it is not yet so rich and economic conditions are not too good."

Beijing was determined to build on its new legal safeguards for the elderly, he said, adding it was in the interests of all. "To honour the old is to honour oneself," he said. "The today of the elderly is my tomorrow."
